summary: The note describes how climate change-driven extreme weather in September 2023 worsened local pollution through ozone smog from heatwaves, stormwater runoff into waterways, and storm debris straining waste management. It quotes local experts on each problem and then covers responses: low-cost air quality monitors, tree-planting campaigns, and individual lifestyle changes such as less driving, rain barrels and recycling.
one_line: Extreme weather in September 2023 increased local air, water and waste pollution, prompting community innovations, tree planting and lifestyle changes.
key_facts: Heatwaves in mid-September 2023 pushed temperatures well into the triple digits and caused ozone levels to skyrocket, creating smog.
On September 18th, Dr. Martin Liu, a local pulmonologist, warned people with respiratory conditions to stay indoors as air quality reached a five-year peak.
Dr. Liu said "Heatwaves expedite the chemical reactions that produce ozone from pollutants."
Dr. Rebecca Harmon of the Clearview Environmental Research Center is cited as a local scientist highlighting climate change's impact on pollution.
Torrential downpours in September overwhelmed the municipality's stormwater management systems, which were designed decades earlier.
On September 23rd, Olivia Sanchez of the Riverfront Conservation Group reported that storm runoff carries chemicals from petroleum products to pesticides into the water supply.

Hank Roberts, the town's Waste Management Coordinator, called managing the post-storm waste influx "a logistical nightmare"; a September storm knocked down trees and scattered debris in the town center.
On September 30th, the GreenTech Startup Hub launched an initiative to develop low-cost air quality monitoring devices giving residents real-time pollution data.
Martha Diaz, a startup leader, said accessible technology helps residents make informed health decisions and hold polluters accountable.

The Urban Forestry Coalition advocates planting more trees and expanding green spaces; its report released October 4th said leafy expanses filter pollutants and cool urban areas, reducing the heat island effect.
The note recommends reducing car usage, installing rain gardens or rain barrels, and using environmentally friendly lawn care products.
Residents are encouraged to recycle and compost using local curbside pickup or community drop-off programs.
